account: Today appears to have been mostly routine town business. The unusual difficulty was locating municipal accounts: the secretary found the four great-hall table chests empty, and I found 128 emeralds but no records in the treasury. I left the public funds untouched. I do not know whether accounts exist elsewhere, so their absence is not evidence of theft. The secretary has been maintaining appointments and relaying messages. The baker and innkeeper asked about gatherings, bread orders and visitors, apparently to plan their business; I know of no planned gathering or expected visitors and authorized no town bread order. My neighbour reported ordinary oven activity, a quiet warehouse and an available ferry, with no damage observed. Freight had told the neighbour that the builder wanted to discuss inspections and paid repairs. I asked the builder for inspection findings and an itemized estimate before any expenditure. He has now come to my home after dark and woken me to report no confirmed damage on the bridge or east-bank routes he walked, lanterns present, and no spending incurred. He intends to inspect the remaining west-bank roads tomorrow. His late visit is notable, but the report itself suggests routine maintenance planning rather than a demonstrated emergency. Tomorrow I should read the appointment book in the office and attend the ten o'clock mill grain inspection.
